author: @GrumpyBulb
text:
I've owned both (Model 3 LR & Seal Excellence) & my short advice to anybody that's considering buying either:

Seats - M3 is comfier for longer even though initially the Seal feels better (not as much under thigh support is the problem I think, the back seats are much better in the Seal than the M3 though)
Performance - M3 accelerator pedal is more snappy / responsive, the Seal's pedal feels slightly muted even in Sport but overall the Seal pushes you back in the seat harder when you give it a bootful
Chassis - M3 is more nimble / tight / agile, the Seal is more comfy & better damped but will wallow more (slightly) into corners as the suspension loads up, you can also feel the extra 400KGs of the Seal
Brakes / Regen braking - M3 brake pedal feels more wooden but you hardly use it due to regen braking, the Seal's pedal has more travel & feels more spongy but does have more feel, it can be grabby at very slow speeds though. You use the brake pedal more on the Seal as the regen braking is less forceful
Controls - M3 gear select & indicators take some getting used to but you do, the touch screen is more responsive & has better resolution, the Seal has had some software updates since this video was done & controls are easy to get to with a bottom, customisable menu on the main screen. I prefer the Seal as it feels more like a "traditional" car, especially with the HUD & digital driver display.
Range / charging - I would regularly trust the M3 to get me home even at 5% projected battery from a long drive, you can trust the projected mileage even at 80mph on the motorway, the Seal has less range than claimed by a long distance & I dont trust the range projected as much as the Tesla. Charging outside of the Tesla Supercharger network is like the Wild West & more expensive. The last update to the Seal now provides suggested charge points on the route but is isn't as good as the Tesla option

Final thought - drive them both, see what you prefer but if range & cost per mile is the most important consideration for you, buy the Tesla. For comparison, I drive my M3 exactly the same as I drove any other ICE car before & it returned 4.3miles/kW over the 9k miles I owned it, the Seal is giving me 3.1 miles/kW in the 3k miles I've had it so far.

author: @AZBuff97
text: I drove a brand new Rolls Royce Ghost.  All the climate controls were knobs, sliders, buttons, etc.  I'll be buying 1 owner used pre-screen vehicles until manufactures re-release controls that you can operate by memory without taking your eyes off the road.  Also, screen menus are slow and cumbersome.  Imagine how frustrated people are around you when you are focused on your menus (parking for example).  Amazing how all those years we successfully parked our cars without screens/cameras.  It was a skill driver's needed to learn.  Range loss and charge time continue to be the primary factors for widespread EV adoption.   We drove some Teslas 460 miles in the Colorado Mountains, with a mix of mountain passes, canyons, state highway cruising, and interstate at 75+.  We had to charge 3 times for about 45 minutes each charge.  And the charging stations had no services (bathroom, food, etc.).  Just parking lots and chargers.  In the heat of summer the range loss is around 50%.  The use case for EV's is still limited.

author: @BerndPaysan
text:
I tested Tesla Model 3 (before facelift) and BYD Seal, and with the 3YO and wife on the backseat.  The 3YO puked in the Tesla when driving around curvy roads, and falls asleep in the BYD seal.  The update notice that came before you did your test said they had added a drift mode, and that's probably what you have seen.  It's only available in sports mode, and you can improve it by turning off ESC mode (it's not completely off, it will kick in at above 80km/h if the drifting gets out of control).  I use Eco and normal mode, and don't use sports mode, and haven't seen anything like that, i.e. on normal driving conditions.  Well, I also replaced the EcoContact 6 tires with Michelin CrossClimate 2, and they do have better grip in cold wet conditions.
Overall, both braking pedals (not much force required) and steering wheel feel Citroën-like (DIRAVI style with no feedback but speed-dependent force), and might take some time to get used to.  I had a Citroën before, so I felt at home.  While the brakes needed to be pushed gently, the accelerator needs to be pushed deliberately to get full power.  Generally, the BYD the way more comfortable car, compared to the Model 3 before facelift.  Also, Elon Musk makes it really, really difficult to buy a product.  I mean, as former Citroën driver, I celebrate JP Boulanger for resisting the Nazis, so how on earth could I buy a car from a Nazi?

author: @Cloud__ffvii
text:
BYD Seal Excellence owner here, my views are this:

- It’s very fast off the line, not so much at higher speeds, cuts off at 120mph
- Looks amazing inside and out 
- Very comfortable to drive 
- Lots of gadgets and settings that take getting used to; once you’ve got it set up and understand it all it’s fine, only issue is traffic warning needs turning off each time 
- Stereo system is great
- Voice control for most features
- Apple Car Play is great, getting a 3rd party bridge Carlinkit to make full screen mirror and other app use to work eg Netflix / YouTube 
- The front parking sensors are useless, kick in at 50cm (but if you look it’s much less than 50cm imo)
- Rear parking sensors too quiet 
- Range is nowhere near what they say. I drove in eco, standard range (not dynamic), turned AC off, turned screen off, brake regen on high and a 20 mile journey knocked 40 miles off my battery; perhaps in warmer weather it’ll be less noticeable 

It’s a great car all in all though, real head turner, you won’t see many about and it’ll leave a dual motor Tesla M for dust at take off from traffic lights, unless it’s the performance model.

author: @artCeptual
text:
The new interface in the Model 3 is ghastly.  I hate the indicators as the controls don't fit my driving style.  But, the previous generate Model 3 (while a bit bumpier in the back seats and a tiny bit louder) is immense fun.  I ordinarily dislike single track rural roads with lumps of horse excrement in the middle, with the phrase "risk of grounding" floating continually in my mind, but the Tesla makes driving even those horrible roads fun and easy.  HOWEVER, the Model 3 needs an update to its camera lenses: they need either a rotating ball, and/or a cleaning solution.  They also need high definition night cameras because if you get caught in a country lane, as I have, and need to reverse, then all you can rely on are your mirrors (in an unlit lane with stone walls either side), or your cameras which only show you where your going when the brake lights come on as you inevitably panic about scratching your lovely new car, while simultaneously annoying the local who has driven the stretch of road a million times, in a tractor, and could easily let a coach get through.  This, as a result, can make a reasonably good driver *appear* thick.  Those are my main criticisms.

Oh, and don't take a Tesla Model 3 to a muddy field without "Slip Mode" activated.  I instantly buried 30% of the wheels as a result.  It made me *appear* thick ;)

text:
I drove a BYD Atto as rental in Germany two weeks ago and I am not impressed with the interior. Being 1.9m I had to lower the seat quite a bit, which brings it back and then my left shoulder was at the B-Column, being able to grab the steering wheel only at the bottom left. The acceleration was good, charging quiet fast and the range ok (Munich <> Nuremberg).

Cameras around were a cool feature, but a little bit off. In a small park house, I had to rely on the side mirrors to judge, rather than the camera.

text: I have one of the new Tesla Model 3s. I prefer the minimalist interior, but I agree they've gone too far with the stalk removal. The turn signal buttons are harder to use, especially when the steering wheel is inverted. The gear shifter is awkward, especially in situations where you have to change quickly or often, like parking. I'd even go so far as to say they detract from safety - you have to look at the steering wheel sometimes to locate the turn signal buttons and sometimes it's just easier not to indicate. Several times I've made a mistake with the gear shifter and ended up going in the wrong direction, it's surprisingly easy to do. I still prefer the new 3 to the old one, but you buy it despite the signal buttons and gear shifter, not because of them. I hope they put them back in a future model.

author: @adamselene9264
text:
You Have Problems, Not Issues
Somewhere, at some point over the recent past, someone decided that it was no longer acceptable for a person to say what he or she means; it was no longer acceptable to speak in precise, direct words. And what’s worse, someone, somewhere decided that we should all be offended when someone calls a problem a problem. Everything has to be translated into some sort of euphemism. I don’t really know why it started, but can we please stop referring to every problem as an issue?

An employee no longer has a problem keeping up with production; he has an issue. A child no longer has a problem behaving in class; she has an issue. A married couple in therapy no longer has problems in their marriage; they have issues.

Even bad weather now causes performance issues on the football field and traffic issues on the road; and a basketball player with a sprained ankle has an ankle issue. I’m not sure what’s so offensive about discussing traffic problems, health problems, or a sloppy football game. Is it just me?

The problem—that is, what’s wrong—with substituting issue for problem is that those two words are not synonymous—and no amount of being politically correct, disingenuous, or even condescending—yes, it can be condescending—will make it so.

An issue is a topic, such as The candidates will discuss the issues at the debate. That means that the candidates will discuss the different topics, or subject areas, involved in running our country.

A problem is something negative. A problem is something that needs to be solved. A problem is something that we try to overcome. A problem is something that we don’t want. There, I’ve said it. And it feels great.

An issue is not a problem, but I’ll tell you what is a problem: the grammatically incorrect trend of telling someone that he has an issue when what you really mean is that he has a problem. Call it what it is, and it’ll be easier to solve.

author: @petermalkin2701
text:
I've recently driven both these cars and I totally disagree with this review. 
Yes the Tesla  probably does have better ultimate handling although on the road the difference is very small. The big advantage the Seal has is that has a vastly superior and more comforatble ride quality and it pushes  the Tesla close for handling- certainly on the road and not on a track. The next massive diffeence betwen the cars is that of the finish and build  quality. The Seal is streets ahead  -yes Tesla have improved from a low level but my demonstrator still had average panel gaps and paint finish whilst the Seal was superbly finished and felt much more solid. Another thing to consider is that the Seal uses the latest Lithium Iron Phosphate battery technology which is MUCH more rugged and durable that those of the Tesla.
Finally price - unlike most of the motoring reviewers I live  the North of England where strangely four-wheel-drive is a real positive in poor road  conditions and RWD is a total liability. Hence if you compare these versions and you don't want white paint or 18" wheels the Tesla is almost £4000 more expensive with less kit. 
Its a no-brainer the Seal wins by a mile

author: @FireWalkMusic
text:
Tesla has taken cost cutting too far, and it has now made the car frustrating to drive, sadly. The turn signal buttons on the steering wheel are extremely annoying to use in tight roundabouts, because it forces you to constantly look down at the wheel in a critical situation when your eyes really should be on the road. It's a safety concern!

They are also not always responsive, and will require you to try again. It is also far to easy to press the wrong button. You will know if you pressed a stalk up or down, but you have no way of knowing if you pressed the correct button, unless you take your eyes off the road again and look down when pressing, or at the screen to confirm.

The wiper button is also moved to the wheel, which I don't like. Wouldn't have been a problem if the auto wipers were the best in the business, but they're not. In fact they're the worst, so you're going to be using that manual wiper button a lot.. 
The AP button is also unresponsive at times. It doesn't always register double taps, even though I can clearly hear it clicks twice. And the high beams also automatically comes on when engaging the AP, blinding other cars, so you constantly have to turn them off. 

I can live with the gear selector on the screen, but honestly, this too is a downgrade. Particularly in tight parking garages for example, when you need to do a lot of back and forward motion. Before you could change direction while looking around at the same time. Now you have to look at the screen to swipe instead, so it's more tedious and slower than before, and it makes you less aware of your surroundings. 
All this just makes the car really annoying to drive, particularly when there are tight roundabouts everywhere, which tend to be the case here in the EU. 

They also removed the ultrasonic parking sensors, and the new camera-based system is so inaccurate that it's basically useless now. Fog lights are also removed, and I also miss a dedicated instrument cluster or a HUD. Apparently they're now also going to downgrade the stereo to just 7 speakers. What's next? Virtual steering wheel on the screen? That would surely make the car even cheaper!

It's just sad that they've opted to remove so many useful functions to cut costs, because the rest of the car is actually great, but due to these stupid decisions it becomes frustrating to drive, and I don't like spending good money on a car that constantly annoys me...

If they had kept the stalks, added a instrument cluster, and kept the ultrasonic parking sensors and the fog lights the car would have been almost perfect.

They might have the cheaper car, but I think most people would gladly pay a little bit more to get back those missing features..

author: @jonsykes8780
text:
I guess the lack of  a central speedo or HUD explains why Teslas are driven at either 50mph in the middle lane of the motorway or 70 mph on residential roads. The drivers have no idea what speed they are travelling.

As for the bright white seats, I suppose the majority of Teslas are driven by company reps who don't have kids. And the two grand for a colour explains why so many are white, company fleet managers won't pay for that.

The lack of physical controls is a massive red flag for me. No car should take weeks or months to learn to drive. A few days for the idiosyncrasies of the lesser used controls maybe. But indicators, gears/drive selectors etc should be second nature the instant you get  behind the wheel. I don't want fart apps. I don't want Mario kart rip off games. 

I want a safe car that myself and other members of my family can just drive without having to refer to the owners manual just to put it in reverse.

Just about every review that mentions EV in general or Tesla specifically will mention the wonders of the supercharger network. Well, for me, it's a benefit that's of little use. I don't work hundreds of miles from home. I don't have to travel for work. In the 18 months we've owned an EV, I've plugged it into a public charger once, just to see how it worked. It worked fine. I charge at home, far cheaper than any public network, so you can keep your wonder network, it's no use to me.

We have two cars. One a small city EV, the other a diesel 4x4. Neither of these EVs are suitable replacements for ours. Tesla do not make a car than can replace either. They don't do small city cars and their attempts at an SUV is the laughable Model X. Stupid rear doors that mean you can't put cycles on the roof, stupidly expensive and virtually every Model X on the UK Tesla website, when selecting the New car option, is an ex-Demo car. I've never seen any other manufacturer class ex-Demo cars with thousands of miles on the clock as New.  Oh, and the final feature of the Model X in the UK? "Only available as left-hand drive".

Auto-pilot that isn't New cars that aren't new. Steering wheel on the wrong side. Why do people like Tesla?

author: @gfbrittoncarlisle
text:
Tesla ruined the Model 3 with the new steering wheel. I hate the new wheel designs and I wouldn’t ever buy one that was missing surround cameras, parking sensors, adaptive dampers, HUD, or cross traffic detection. Tesla is also falling behind on the charging speeds against cars like the Ioniq 6. As a former Model 3P owner there’s just not enough new to make me excited about the Highland 3. My 2019 3P had more hardware than the brand new one and I didn’t have to rely on the unreliable cameras to judge how close I was to objects. Tesla vision is horrendously unreliable. My experience in multiple recent Ys and 3s has confirmed Tesla Vision has no idea how close objects are in reality. It often sees phantom things or doesn’t see things at all. Elon needs to stop taking features out.  The vast majority of Model 3 owners do not care about having a small display for passengers in the rear. A basic climate control panel with buttons for heated seats would’ve been just fine and cheaper. Instead, as I mentioned, I’m sure the average consumer would much rather have more cameras, radar front and rear for cross traffic detection, a HUD, driver display, or massaging seats instead. For this, the BYD is a better buy, but I would go for an Ioniq 6, Ioniq 5N, EV6 GT or i4 before I bought either of these.

Also, Mat, the 10-80% charge in a Model 3 is about 28 minutes, not 14. The car doesn’t maintain 250kW for more than a few minutes. By 50% it’s dropped down to around 125kW. By 80% you’re below 80kW. The fastest charging cars from 10-80% are the Hyundai/Kia/Genesis e-GMP cars that offer an 18 minute charge time.

text:
I think the biggest question you would have to ask yourself if deciding between these two cars is: "Do I want to support a company from China (which has some serious political and humanitarian issues) or Elon Musk (who has some serious political and humanitarian issues)?" I guess if you have kids or dogs it might get dirtier but for an average adult I have not had an issue.

author: @ganymede3141
text: @ronnythompson9115 Gear controls on the rearview mirror? 😂 Why not just put them in the trunk where they're more convenient? And app? The app can only do a few basic functions like door lock/unlock, open frunk and trunk, honk the horn, and climate control. But everything else would be gone. You won't be opening the trunk or frunk or locking/unlocking doors while you're driving, and having to use your phone for ANYTHING while driving ia just a really bad idea. My point was that the screen is a single point of failure, the avoidance of which is Engineering 101. Doing it DELIBERATELY is just idiotic. But my main point was, why complicate something simple like a stalk by now shoving that functionality into a touch screen that requires software and all sorts of other unnecessary complications and failure mechanisms. What was wrong with the stalk? Nothing. Absolutely nothing. It was functional, ergonomic, easy to use, simple, and reliable. Leave it to Tesla to take something simple and overcomplicate it for overcomplication's sake. Same thing happened with the asinine yoke. When it was initially offered, Elon said a regular steering wheel option would not be offered. After many reviewers and owners discovered just how useless and pain in the ass it was and complained about the useless change that was for looks only, Tesla quietly made the round steering wheel the default option on the S and X, with the yoke now being a $1000 option. Because the round steering wheel has been around for over a century, and it has been around for that long because it WORKS and is practical. I predict the same will happen with this swipe to shift feature. By introducing it on a high-volume car like the Model 3, mainstream buyers will be turned off by the swipe to shift and capacitive turn signals, and in a few years the stalks will be back when sales plummet. If it happened with the yoke, it'll happen with this. People will vote with their wallets.

author: @daveromanyshyn1170
text: This is my opinion on Tesla versus non-Tesla EV ownership and is based on living in the US. I had a 22' Model 3 and I currently have a Ford lightning ev. Here's how I'd summarize Tesla versus non-tesla if you're looking into your first ev. If you just want to get in and drive on a trip and not worry about charging on trips, your only option is a Tesla. The software takes care of everything and you don't have to think about it charging. If you plan on taking long trips in a non-tesla, the software doesn't take the thinking out of it. You have to be willing to take time before your trip to research chargers on your trip. You have to be willing to download apps for various charging companies to be able to pay for them. You have to be able to download other navigation apps (eg ABRP as well since the in-car navigation isn't always reliable when it comes to chargers. If you are a tech geek like me, or willing to put a little bit of time and effort into it, you can get a non-tesla and make it work. If, however, you don't want to do any of that or you don't know how to do any of that, currently Tesla with its supercharging station and it's game-changing software is literally the only game in town worth considering. They are so far ahead with their charging infrastructure and software it's not even funny. As far as the quirks including the buttonless interior, the big Central screen, the weird door handles, you will get used to that. You don't even think about looking at the speedometer in the center of the car. Only car reviewers who get in and out of a dozen different cars each week whine about that stuff.

text: May just be me, but I find both of these cars awful. I've been a passenger in several EV's ranging from a model S (which I also got to drive) to a Kia EV6 and Chevy Bolt...and I didnt really click with any of them. I mean sure the first time you experience the acceleration (Tesla and Kia, not so much the Chevy) it's pretty cool...but the reality is most people dont have a drag strip on their daily commute and I find most EV drivers settle into driving normally after the new wears off..especially those trying to avoid more charging time. I may be a purist, but I find the interior of both these cars to be more boring and sterile than cool and futuristic. I have an ipad that I like to use, but I dont care to have it in my car controlling normal functions better left to buttons, knobs and levers. Meh, guess I'm just glad I live in the U.S. where we still have a chance for sanity to prevail. What do I mean by that? EV's for sale to those who want them, but also ICE/ICE hybrids as well...at least until EV tech matures enough that all of the current drawbacks are mostly eliminated. I simply wouldnt trust any EV as my only personal vehicle, and I live in a part of the U.S. where personal transport is more than just a luxury.

author: @GrevMarkussen
text:
I’ve had a Model 3 for a couple of years (2019), and I like it! But to evaluate it properly, you have to remember how cheap it, and the Model Y, is (for the amount of range etc. you get) - because you can absolutely feel the cheapness! But I don’t mind when I have that frame of mind. 

Many of the things improved in the facelift is things I’d like on my car - but the removal of the stalks is a complete dealbreaker (they’ve also removed the sensors on the bumpers, compared to mine! 🤦🏻‍♂️). Especially using indicators in roundabouts seems terrible… I actually don’t miss head-up display at all (and you get get aftermarket ones), and you can (on my old version) do anything regarding cruise control, gears, wipers, radio, etc. from the wheel. 

There’s also a specific reason I don’t miss CarPlay/Android Auto: Those systems can’t get info about the battery. Why is this important? Last winter I drove from Norway to France - and I could just put in where I wanted to go in the navigation, and it knew when I had to charge. It also pre-heated the batteries when charging was near. You just can’t do that with 3rd party stuff at the moment, so I prefer a good 1st party system. (But it should hopefully be sorted!)

author: @TheSerbianEmperor
text:
I really despise the recent modern trend of making everything "elegant" with swipes, touch screens, gestures and capacitive buttons. I'll agree, it does look futuristic, sometimes even improves the looks, minimalistic aesthetics, etc. ,but why reinvent the wheel, literally in case of Tesla? If your change doesn't make a genuine improvement then don't change it at all, but don't remove features and replace them with worse ones.
Simplicity and intuitiveness of mechanical buttons and switches is brilliant! Everyone knows how they work, you don't need a course on how to use them. Engaging, disengaging and turning things off and on without looking is not only easier, but much, much safer for the driver.
Having absolutely everything in your car tied to literally one failure point, the center screen in Tesla, is mind-blowingly idiotic. If the screen dies for whatever reason, glitches, mechanical, physical or software damage, your car is dead. Why that is still a thing is crazy, and what's even more crazy is that it happens more and more. Cars are devolving instead of evolving, and everything else is too.

author: @juergenvonhausberg
text:
There are some contextual mistakes here. Tesla autopilot (which is included with every car), does not have autoparking. It has nothing to do with recall. Recall was anyways about driver monitoring and nags - nothing to do with this. Autoparking is, AFAIK with 7k Full Self Driving option. 
There is also something about smart summon option, which I believe is currently disabled since omitting the ultrasonic sensors. You are also lacking the new updated 3D view in Tesla, which came with Christmas update. Should make that parking exercise easier.

As for the stalks and buttons or gear change with the screen. I have had the new version for 3 months now. I do not notice them anymore. I am not a huge fan of the blinker buttons, but they do not disturb me, maybe cause I am a former BMW driver. As for the gears, I am happy with the change and I love the automatic gear engament, not much use in parking and back and forth, though.

You might have said a word about acoustics. Tesla got a huge improvement with model update and also, the ventilated seats is a nice add.

Now, as for the HUD and generally optional stuff. Tesla does not make cars for individual order. They manufacture a mass model with statistical distribution of different colours. That is how they manage low production costs, insane production speed and high volumes. Gimmicks will make a difference once the market is filled. HUD take-rates  in something like BMW are less than 10% and all the reviewers and commentators go apesh!t as if everybody needs one, has one and can afford one. Sod it.

text:
@Popdog76 Unfortunately, that is marketing and the numbers they quite assume the best case scenario.  That is, "highway speed" as defined by the EPA in the U.S., which has a maximum speed for the test - BRIFELY - of 59.9mph. The average is about 50mph.  All figures for Tesla are simply copied over and converted for the U.K. market. 
The real-world range in cold (below freezing) weather of a Model 3 is 30% less.  Simple physics. But turning on the heat and having extra passengers can rob closer to 35% of the range.  Where in an ICE vehicle, it's largely moot at a couple of tenths of a MPG and the heating is just waste heat that is diverted.  Add in that you are charging from an 80% state to a 20% state to prolong battery life and back up to 80% and your range can indeed be 150 miles.  You can push it, but your battery won't last much beyond 100K miles.

author: @Paul-ow9dd
text:
The BYD Seal is a great car, I've driven 2 of the 3 models available in Australia, the mid-range Premium 230kw RWD and also the scarily powerful Performance 390kw AWD (Excellence in the UK) In Australia the Seal is better value than the Tesla, and much cheaper than in the UK.
I paid a $1000 deposit and ordered a Seal with the option to purchase either the RWD or the AWD. I had concerns before seeing the Seal in person and test driving it that its ground clearance may be an issue. YES IT IS! On my steep driveway where the sloping entrance intersects the flat concrete of my carport. In an unladen Seal there is only 2 centimetres of clearance from the leading edge of the front bumper and the concrete. No where near enough clearance. I was guaranteed to scrape the underside of the front bumper. I was also concerned about some speed humps and how it would go on unsealed and poorly maintained roads. I imagine the black plastic bottom of the Seals front bumper would be very expensive to replace. It looks replaceable as it is screwed in place, but spare parts are usually horrendously overpriced.

Please take this into consideration before forking out for a Seal.

The Model 3 Highland has 6 centimetres of clearance in my problematic driveway. Not a huge amount but quite doable if I take it very slow in and out of my carport. My current 2015 VW Polo has 5 centimetres of clearance. That car like many ICE vehicles has a sacrificial flexible plastic band across the underside of the bumper sticking down about 3 centimetres which gives you a warning that clearance is low, without scraping the actual bumper. NO such warning in the BYD OR Tesla.

The rotating screen in the Seal and Atto isn't all gimmick. It's good in portrait mode for using navigation and "looking ahead" to where your going.

Tesla software is better. The Seal uses an old version of Android and is a bit clunky to use. The Seal (and Atto 3) ADAS system "bings and bongs" as the safety driving features are oversensitive - more so than the Tesla. So, the wheel in the Seal vibrates too much and the noisy sounds get a bit annoying and lane assist can be quite scary. Hopefully future OTA updates will improve things.

Last week I ordered a Model 3 RWD. Today after MORE exhaustive research (and before watching this review) I changed my order to the LR AWD Model 3. Can't wait for delivery! 🙂 Should be a good compliment to the wife's lot more sedate Atto 3.

I'm sure I'll get used to the indicators on the steering wheel. Tesla should have only put those on the US market version. Like the UK we have too many roundabouts here in Australia, so it should be a whole lot of fun indicating to exit a roundabout. LOL!

As in the ENTIRE vehicle - almost like it's a special effect in the paint.  Except it's a defect that the industry knows how to keep from happening. author: @plektosgaming
text: @ilyarepin7750 At high speeds your field of view narrows.  Say, at 70-80mph.  There are many highways in the U.S. and Europe that are at this speed.  It narrows enough such that the number showing your speed in the Model 3 is just outside of that cone.  So essentially, at speed, every time you look at the speed, it's as if you are briefly texting as you have to completely re-focus.  This is why HUDs are infinitely safer, especially at night. And we're talking about a $200 unit that they could put in - it just needs to display the basics.  Now, if it was like the new S class AR HUD, that would be what we expect given that there's nothing there aside from a wheel.

author: @GBO-UA
text:
@Carwow Guys, you are cool and do a great job entertaining the viewers, but these tests have the same value as grown-up boys competing on wee-wee dimensions. These EVs will never use this acceleration in normal life, but let them make at least 2-3 turns and measure the tires' temperature. How do they look underneath: suspension, corrosion, and impact protection? Can we purchase a bumper, headlight, or a fender if damaged, and find it new, not jeopardized from damaged ones? Value comparison in 3 years and 50,000 km. Energy efficiency and how they behave in winter with all necessary accessories functioning as they should.

I watch these overviews with great frustration, as the refined and good-working technology of internal combustion is neglected in favor of another tech that has not proven to be reliable, self-sustaining, and refined.

I live and work in Ukraine. I have met the russian invasion in bed and been woken up by the explosions. These days, the country with 40 million populations began to evacuate their relatives and families away from the danger. Imagine the situation when you have to drive 400-500 km without a stop in cold weather (February), the car is fully loaded with people and their belongings, and then, in the middle of nowhere, it is found out that the battery is almost dead. You take your children, your old parents and walk away from the danger. A month later you face a situation of total blackout that lasted not for days but for months. The only way to charge the vehicle is to buy diesel oil and start the generator... very environmentally friendly.

The EV technology is far from the point where we could say it is self-sufficient, but at the same moment, the decision-makers are pushing hard to kill the internal combustion engine: I know enough cases when car manufacturers have closed any research related to IC and fired the technicians... a very short-sighted decision, but in the end, neither the politician nor the decision-maker would pay the consequences from their pockets. The only thing they can say: "Sorry, I was wrong.

I'll agree, it does look futuristic, sometimes even improves the looks, minimalistic aesthetics, etc. ,but why reinvent the wheel, literally in case of Tesla? If your change doesn't make a genuine improvement then don't change it at all, but don't remove features and replace them with worse ones.
Simplicity and intuitiveness of mechanical buttons and switches is brilliant! Everyone knows how they work, you don't need a course on how to use them. Engaging, disengaging and turning things off and on without looking is not only easier, but much, much safer for the driver.
Having absolutely everything in your car tied to literally one failure point, the center screen in Tesla, is mind-blowingly idiotic. If the screen dies for whatever reason, glitches, mechanical, physical or software damage, your car is dead. Why that is still a thing is crazy, and what's even more crazy is that it happens more and more. Cars are devolving instead of evolving, and everything else is too.

author: @NicoSchurr
text: @tsh4k it is an imperfect measurement, sure. It measures the quality of the charging cycle as fully as is reasonable but says little about road tripping ability. The other increasingly used measurement is range gained in 15 minutes of charging, assuming 15 minutes as an acceptable charging stop. Eventually, cars will be able to make sufficient range gains in less than 15 minutes and then this measurement will be outdated once again. The issue with both the "range gained in an x min stop" and the "time to gain x amount of miles" is: which efficiency figure should be used. We all know WLTP combined is far from the reality of road tripping and there is no other official standard that could be used by the industry.
